kurals.tamil:
ஒற்றும் உரைசான்ற நூலும் இவையிரண்டும்
தெற்றென்க மன்னவன் கண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Otrum uraisaandra noolum ivaiyirandum
Thetrenga mannavan kan.
kurals.meaning: A ruler should clearly understand that he has two eyes: his spies, who show him what is actually happening, and the respected books of law, which show him what ought to be done.
kurals.elementary: A captain steering a ship needs two things: a lookout who shouts what he sees on the sea, and a map that shows the right route. With only one, the ship gets lost. This kural says a ruler is the same: he needs people who tell him what is really going on, and good rules that tell him what is right.
kurals.university: The chapter title ஒற்றாடல் means ‘the employment (ஆடல், handling) of spies’; one printed text glosses it ஒற்றரை ஆளும் திறம், ‘the skill of managing spies’. It follows directly on கண்ணோட்டம் (ch. 58, ‘the kindly eye’), and Valluvar continues the eye image by naming two organs of royal sight: ஒற்று (the spy, or intelligence generally) and உரைசான்ற நூல் (a treatise ‘full of renown’). Parimelazhagar takes the second to be the science of polity (நீதிநூல்), and the commentators draw the contrast that the treatise shows what should be done while the spy shows what is being done; a king lacking either is half-blind. The verb தெற்றென்க (‘let him know clearly’) turns the saying into a direct order. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it the same way, and the text is identical on ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and thirukkural-thamizh.org, the last printing it in older sandhi-joined form (ஒற்று முரைசான்ற நூலு மிவையிரண்டுந்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let the king who sees (everything) through his spies, discover the two sorts of thieves who deprive others of their property, both those who (show themselves) openly and those who (lie) concealed.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu describes the ideal king as one who ‘sees through his spies’ (the Sanskrit ideal of the cāra-cakṣus, the spy-eyed ruler) and uses that sight to apply the law against open and hidden wrongdoers.
hinduism.tie_back: Spies as the king’s eyes, working together with the law, is exactly the Kural’s pair of ‘two eyes’.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close parallel; Manu names the spy-eye explicitly, and the law is implied by the context rather than called a second eye.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For the word of God is quick, and powerful … and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart. Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews joins a searching, discerning word to an all-seeing eye from which nothing is hidden.
christianity.tie_back: A discerning word plus a seeing eye mirrors the Kural’s law-book plus spy, though here both belong to God and not to a king.
christianity._accuracy_note: Thematic match on word and sight together; the passage is theological, not about statecraft.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, We have revealed to you, [O Muḥammad], the Book in truth so you may judge between the people by that which Allāh has shown you. And do not be for the deceitful an advocate.”
islam.explanation: The ruler-judge is to decide by the revealed Book and by what God has let him see, and is warned against being fooled into siding with deceivers.
islam.tie_back: The Book and the ‘showing’ together play the roles of the Kural’s law-text and spy-eye.
islam._accuracy_note: Clear on law guiding judgment; the ‘seeing’ element comes from God rather than from human informants.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A king that sitteth in the throne of judgment scattereth away all evil with his eyes.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs pictures a king on the seat of justice whose watchful sight alone drives wrongdoing away.
judaism.tie_back: Judgment (law) and the king’s eyes are the two instruments of the Kural’s couplet.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on royal sight joined to judgment; says nothing of spies as the means of seeing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Cakkavatti-Sīhanāda Sutta, the righteous wheel-turning king is told to rely on the Dhamma alone, to give lawful protection to all classes, and to go regularly to wise ascetics and ask them what is wholesome and what is not, so that he stays informed and on the right path.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist ideal king governs by two supports: the Dhamma as his law and constant questioning of the wise as his source of knowledge.
buddhism.tie_back: Law plus active inquiry is a gentler Buddhist version of the Kural’s law-book plus spy.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the two-support structure, but the inquiry is moral consultation, not espionage.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says that the maiden Dike (Justice) sits beside her father Zeus and tells him of men’s unjust minds, and that the eye of Zeus sees all and understands all.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Greek picture, the king of the gods rules with two helpers: Justice, who reports wrongdoing, and his own all-seeing eye.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Justice and the watching eye beside the throne match the Kural’s law and spy as a king’s two eyes.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close structural parallel; Dike is a divine reporter and not a hired spy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Xenophon says that Cyrus the Great, by rewarding everyone who brought him useful information, came to have many so-called ‘King’s eyes’ and ‘King’s ears’ spread across his empire, so that people feared to say or do anything against him.
philosophy.explanation: Xenophon presents a network of informants as the sense organs of a well-run empire.
philosophy.tie_back: The ‘King’s eyes’ are the Kural’s ஒற்று almost word for word.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on spies as eyes; Xenophon does not pair them with a law-book.

kurals.tamil:
எல்லார்க்கும் எல்லாம் நிகழ்பவை எஞ்ஞான்றும்
வல்லறிதல் வேந்தன் தொழில்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ellaarkkum ellaam nigazhpavai enjnjaandrum
Vallaridhal vaendhan thozhil.
kurals.meaning: It is a king’s job to learn quickly, at all times, everything that happens to everyone, whether enemies, friends or neutrals.
kurals.elementary: A good school principal wants to know right away if someone is being bullied, if a pipe is leaking, or if a new student feels lost, not a month later. This kural says a ruler’s real work is the same: always finding out quickly what is happening to everyone.
kurals.university: The couplet stacks three universals, எல்லார்க்கும் (to all persons), எல்லாம் (all things) and எஞ்ஞான்றும் (at all times), then adds வல் (‘swiftly’) to அறிதல் (knowing). Parimelazhagar spells out ‘all persons’ as the king’s enemies, friends and neutrals (பகைவர், நட்பினர், நொதுமலர்), and Pappaiah and Kalaignar follow this three-way division, which matches the Arthashastra’s mandala theory of foreign relations. Most commentators add ‘through spies’ in brackets because the chapter context requires it, even though the word ஒற்று is not in the line. The closing தொழில் (‘occupation, duty’) presents knowing as the king’s trade and not something he does now and then. The wording is the same on all three sources consulted; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi form எல்லார்க்கு மெல்லா.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As the Wind moves (everywhere), entering (in the shape of the vital air) all created beings, even so let him penetrate (everywhere) through his spies; that is the office in which he resembles the Wind.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu compares the king to the wind god, whose ‘office’ is to reach every being through his spies.
hinduism.tie_back: Getting everywhere, into everyone’s affairs, is the Kural’s ‘all things of all people’; both texts call it the king’s office or duty.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one, including the idea of a royal ‘office’; speed is not stressed.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Watch ye therefore: for ye know not when the master of the house cometh, at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning … And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus demands watchfulness at every hour of the night, because what matters may arrive at any time.
christianity.tie_back: Being alert at every hour echoes the Kural’s எஞ்ஞான்றும், ‘at all times’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the constant-vigilance theme only; it is eschatological, not political intelligence.

islam.quote_or_event: “And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him. And He knows what is on the land and in the sea. Not a leaf falls but that He knows it.”
islam.explanation: The Quran describes God’s complete knowledge of everything that happens, down to a single falling leaf.
islam.tie_back: The Kural asks the human king to aim, as far as he can, at the same complete knowledge of events in his realm.
islam._accuracy_note: Divine omniscience is a model, not a method; the verse is about God, not rulers.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And see the land, what it is; and the people that dwelleth therein, whether they be strong or weak, few or many; And what the land is that they dwell in, whether it be good or bad; and what cities they be that they dwell in, whether in tents, or in strong holds.”
judaism.explanation: Moses gives the twelve spies a full intelligence brief covering people, strength, numbers, land and fortifications.
judaism.tie_back: Moses wants to know ‘everything about everyone’ in Canaan, which is the scope the Kural sets for a king.
judaism._accuracy_note: Direct spy-mission parallel; it is one mission and not the constant watch the Kural describes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Mahā-Ummagga Jātaka the Bodhisatta, as the sage Mahosadha, sends spies to every royal court, and they bring home reports that let him learn of plots against his king before they happen.
buddhism.explanation: The future Buddha is shown as a wise minister who keeps his king informed by a wide network of agents.
buddhism.tie_back: Reports from every court, arriving continually, are the Kural’s ideal of knowing all things about all parties.
buddhism.source: Mahā-Ummagga Jātaka (Jātaka 546), as summarised in the Dictionary of Pali Proper Names (paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel; checked against a reference summary, not the full Cowell translation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hera set Argus Panoptes, the ‘all-seeing’ giant with eyes all over his body, to watch without rest, because some of his eyes were always awake while others slept.
greek_mythology.explanation: Argus is Greek myth’s image of a watcher who never stops seeing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His sleepless, many-eyed watch pictures the Kural’s demand for knowing everything at all times.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A good image of constant surveillance, but Argus guards one captive for a goddess and does not inform a ruler.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Now this foreknowledge cannot be elicited from spirits; it cannot be obtained inductively from experience, nor by any deductive calculation. Knowledge of the enemy’s dispositions can only be obtained from other men.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu argues that the knowledge a sovereign needs most can come only from living informants.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Sun Tzu makes gathering human intelligence a core duty of the wise ruler.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 13.5-6 (trans. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in purpose; Sun Tzu focuses on the enemy, while the Kural covers friends and neutrals as well.

kurals.tamil:
ஒற்றினான் ஒற்றிப் பொருள்தெரியா மன்னவன்
கொற்றங் கொளக்கிடந்தது இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Otrinaan otrip poruldheriyaa mannavan
Kotrang kolakkidandhadhu il.
kurals.meaning: A king who does not gather news through spies and work out what it means has no path to victory.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a football coach who never watches the other team play and never thinks about what their moves mean. He will keep losing. This kural says a leader has to find out what is going on and then think carefully about what it means.
kurals.university: The first line repeats the root ஒற்று (ஒற்றினான் ஒற்றி, ‘spying by means of a spy’), a figure of repetition that runs through the whole chapter. The key phrase is பொருள் தெரியா, ‘not discerning the meaning or import’. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as not examining the benefit (பயன்) of what spies report, and Pulavar Kesikan as not working out the significance of events in enemy lands. So Valluvar is not satisfied with collecting data; the king must interpret it. The second line, கொற்றங் கொளக்கிடந்தது இல், says literally that ‘there is nothing lying there for him to take as victory’. Pappaiah widens கொற்றம் from battlefield victory to lasting success of the government. The text agrees on all three sources; thirukkural-thamizh.org prints ஒற்றினா னொற்றிப் பொருடெரியா, with the sandhi shown.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “By spies, by a (pretended) display of energy, and by carrying out (various) undertakings, let the king constantly ascertain his own and his enemy’s strength.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the king to measure his own strength and the enemy’s constantly, and spies come first among the means.
hinduism.tie_back: ‘Ascertaining strength’ from spy reports is the Kural’s பொருள் தெரிதல், discerning what the intelligence means.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close; Manu does not state the Kural’s negative consequence (no victory) outright.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the example of a king who weighs the enemy’s strength against his own before going to war.
christianity.tie_back: Sitting down to weigh the facts is the interpretive step without which, the Kural says, victory is impossible.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good on assessing before acting; spies are not mentioned, and the parable’s point is the cost of discipleship.

islam.quote_or_event: Before Badr, the Prophet’s scouts brought in two water-carriers of the Quraysh. Asked how many camels the army slaughtered each day, they said nine one day and ten the next, and the Prophet concluded that the enemy numbered between nine hundred and a thousand.
islam.explanation: The early biographies show the Prophet turning a small piece of scouting information into an accurate estimate of enemy numbers.
islam.tie_back: Getting information and then reasoning out its meaning is exactly what the Kural means by ஒற்றிப் பொருள் தெரிதல்.
islam.source: Ibn Ishaq, Sīrat Rasūl Allāh, Battle of Badr (paraphrase)
islam._accuracy_note: Excellent illustration; it comes from sira literature, not from Qur’an or canonical hadith text.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And they brought up an evil report of the land which they had searched unto the children of Israel, saying, The land … is a land that eateth up the inhabitants thereof; and all the people that we saw in it are men of a great stature.”
judaism.explanation: Ten of the twelve spies turned their observations into a fearful, distorted report. The people accepted it without weighing it against Joshua and Caleb’s account and lost their chance to enter the land.
judaism.tie_back: This is a clear case of intelligence gathered but wrongly interpreted, and the promised victory is lost, as the Kural warns.
judaism._accuracy_note: A strong negative example; the failure is the people’s faith and judgment rather than a king’s.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “No harm, indeed, can be done to the Vajjis in battle by Magadha’s king, Ajatasattu, except through treachery or discord.”
buddhism.explanation: King Ajatasattu sent his chief minister Vassakara to find out the Buddha’s view before attacking the Vajjis. Vassakara drew this strategic conclusion from what he heard.
buddhism.tie_back: The minister gathers information and then works out what it means for victory, which is the two-step process the Kural requires.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahāparinibbāna Sutta 1.5 (trans. Sister Vajira & Francis Story)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Real intelligence-gathering episode, but the Buddha’s own teaching was about a republic’s welfare, not war strategy.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On a night raid, Odysseus and Diomedes capture the Trojan scout Dolon, question him about where the Trojan allies are camped, and use his answers to reach the newly arrived Thracian king Rhesus and take his famous horses.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Doloneia shows scouting turned straight into success once the Greeks grasp what the information reveals, namely an unguarded new ally.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Greeks’ success comes from reading the intelligence correctly, which is the Kural’s condition for victory.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clear parallel; the episode also involves the killing of a captive, which the Kural does not address.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles. If you know yourself but not the enemy, for every victory gained you will also suffer a defeat.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu’s best-known saying makes knowledge of the enemy a condition of reliable victory.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural says the same thing from the negative side: without understood intelligence there is no victory.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 3.18 (trans. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near-identical logic; Sun Tzu does not name spies in this line.

kurals.tamil:
வினைசெய்வார் தம்சுற்றம் வேண்டாதார் என்றாங்கு
அனைவரையும் ஆராய்வது ஒற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Vinaiseyvaar thamsutram vaendaadhaar endraangu
Anaivaraiyum aaraaivadhu otru.
kurals.meaning: A true spy watches everyone without exception: the king’s own officials, his relatives, and his enemies alike.
kurals.elementary: A fair referee watches every player on the field, even the ones from his own town and even his friends. If he only watched one team, the game would be unfair. This kural says a good investigator checks on everyone equally.
kurals.university: Valluvar names three groups: வினைசெய்வார் (those who carry out the king’s business, i.e. officials), தம் சுற்றம் (the king’s own kin), and வேண்டாதார் (those who do not wish him well, i.e. enemies). He then sums them up in அனைவரையும் (‘all of them’). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take தம் to mean the king’s own relatives. Kalaignar reads the couplet as a rule of impartiality for the spy, who must not make exceptions for those he likes or dislikes. Pappaiah modernises the groups as civil servants, the ruling party, the opposition and foreigners, and says the spy reads their inner intent (மனக்கருத்து) from their words and deeds. The couplet is also a definition, ending ‘… is a spy’ (ஒற்று), a form repeated in 585-587. The text agrees across sources, with thirukkural-thamizh.org giving the sandhi form தஞ்சுற்றம்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “… shall be sent by the king to espy in his own country the movements of his ministers, priests, commanders of the army, the heir-apparent, the door-keepers, the officer-in-charge of the harem …”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya sends wandering spies to watch the king’s own highest officers, including his heir, as well as foreign kings.
hinduism.tie_back: Watching officials, family and enemies alike is exactly the Kural’s list of ‘officials, kin and those ill-disposed’.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one, and it even names the heir-apparent; the Arthashastra is harsher in method.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And a man’s foes shall be they of his own household.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns, quoting Micah, that opposition can come from one’s closest relatives.
christianity.tie_back: This is why the Kural does not exempt the king’s kin from scrutiny.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the insight about danger within the household; it is about division over faith, not surveillance.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, indeed, among your spouses and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them. But if you pardon and overlook and forgive - then indeed, Allāh is Forgiving and Merciful.”
islam.explanation: The Quran tells believers that even close family can work against their true interest, and urges watchfulness balanced by forgiveness.
islam.tie_back: Being alert even toward one’s own family is the Kural’s point about including தம் சுற்றம் in the spy’s scope.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the kin element; the verse is spiritual and personal, not about state intelligence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Trust ye not in a friend, put ye not confidence in a guide … For the son dishonoureth the father … a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.”
judaism.explanation: Micah, grieving over a corrupt society, warns that friends, advisers and household members may all prove false.
judaism.tie_back: Friends, advisers and family are the same circle the Kural insists must be watched along with open enemies.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good on untrustworthy insiders; it is a lament, not a policy of surveillance.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigālovāda Sutta the Buddha warns of ‘foes in the guise of friends’: the one who only takes, the one who only talks, the flatterer, and the companion in ruin. He teaches how to recognise each by his conduct.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches lay people to test the conduct of those close to them rather than trusting appearances.
buddhism.tie_back: Judging even friends by their words and deeds is the Kural’s impartial ஆராய்தல் (examination) of all.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Similar discernment about intimates; it is personal ethics, not royal intelligence.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Returning to Ithaca disguised as an old beggar, Odysseus secretly tests his own household (the swineherd Eumaeus, the goatherd Melanthius, the maids, and even his son and wife) to learn who has stayed loyal before he acts.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus acts as his own spy, examining servants, family and enemies before trusting anyone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He covers the Kural’s whole range: workers, kin and hostile suitors are all examined alike.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel; Odysseus spies for himself and does not use an agent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle lists among the devices of tyranny that the ruler tries to know everything his subjects say and do, and employs spies such as the ‘female detectives’ of Syracuse and the eavesdroppers Hiero sent to every gathering.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle treats blanket surveillance of citizens as a mark of the tyrant who fears his people.
philosophy.tie_back: This is a useful contrast: Valluvar’s universal scrutiny belongs to a just king (ch. 55) and is aimed at officials and threats, while Aristotle warns what it becomes in a tyrant’s hands.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Same practice, opposite judgment; included as an honest counterpoint.

kurals.tamil:
கடாஅ உருவொடு கண்ணஞ்சாது யாண்டும்
உகாஅமை வல்லதே ஒற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Kadaaa uruvodu kannanjaadhu yaandum
Ugaaamai valladhae otru.
kurals.meaning: A real spy has an appearance that draws no suspicion, does not flinch under anyone’s gaze, and can never be made to let out his secret anywhere.
kurals.elementary: In a game of hide-and-seek in plain sight, the best player looks totally ordinary, stays calm even when someone stares at them, and never giggles and gives themselves away. This kural says a good spy is like that: ordinary-looking, calm and able to keep a secret.
kurals.university: The couplet names three qualities, and two of its words use the lengthened vowel (அளபெடை): கடாஅ உரு, ‘a form that does not provoke questioning’ (from கடாவுதல், to interrogate), and உகாஅமை, ‘not spilling’ (from உகுத்தல், to let fall, i.e. to leak a secret). In between comes கண் அஞ்சாது, ‘not fearing the eyes’ of suspicious onlookers. Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as not fearing the looks of those who watch him. Pappaiah adds that the spy must hold out whatever method is used on him, naming the four upāyas (sāma, dāna, bheda, daṇḍa: persuasion, bribery, division, force). யாண்டும் (‘anywhere, at any time’) makes the secrecy absolute. The wording agrees across sources; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi கண்ணஞ்சா தியாண்டு முகாஅமை.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Scouting Lanka for Rama, Hanuman shrinks himself to the size of a cat and slips into Ravana’s city at night unnoticed. Later, when he is captured and brought before Ravana, he answers fearlessly and gives away nothing that would harm Rama.
hinduism.explanation: Hanuman is the Indian epic’s model of the ideal scout: disguised, fearless before the enemy king, and loyal.
hinduism.tie_back: An unsuspected form, fearless eyes and a closed mouth are the three marks the Kural lists.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match; Hanuman also openly declares himself Rama’s envoy, which the Kural’s spy would not do.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus sends his disciples into hostile territory and tells them to combine shrewdness with a harmless appearance.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Harmless as doves’ is the unsuspected appearance and ‘wise as serpents’ is the discretion the Kural asks of a spy.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good on appearance and prudence; the disciples are open missionaries, not covert agents.

islam.quote_or_event: “So send one of you with this silver coin of yours to the city and let him look to which is the best of food and bring you provision from it and let him be cautious. And let no one be aware of you.”
islam.explanation: The Sleepers of the Cave send one of their number into a hostile city on an errand, with orders to be careful and give no one any sign of who they are.
islam.tie_back: Moving among others unnoticed and revealing nothing is the Kural’s spy in miniature.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on caution and concealment; the mission is survival, not intelligence-gathering.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But if thou return to the city, and say unto Absalom, I will be thy servant, O king; as I have been thy father’s servant hitherto, so will I now also be thy servant: then mayest thou for me defeat the counsel of Ahithophel.”
judaism.explanation: David sends his friend Hushai back into Absalom’s court as a planted agent who looks like a loyal convert and secretly works for David.
judaism.tie_back: Hushai shows the Kural’s qualities: a form that raises no suspicion, calm before the usurper and his advisers, and a secret never revealed.
judaism._accuracy_note: One of the closest ancient parallels to a covert agent in a hostile court.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who is friendly amidst the hostile, peaceful amidst the violent, and unattached amidst the attached — him do I call a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada praises the person whose calm is not shaken by hostile surroundings.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s spy also has to stay composed and fearless among enemies, though for a worldly purpose.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Only the composure-among-enemies trait matches; the verse describes an arahant, not an agent.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On the day he is born, the infant Hermes steals Apollo’s cattle, disguises the tracks with strange sandals and by driving the herd backwards, then lies in his cradle looking innocent and denies everything to Apollo’s face.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hermes, god of messengers and stealth, shows innocent looks, nerve under questioning, and a refusal to confess.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The same three traits make the Kural’s ideal spy, though Hermes uses them for mischief.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Matches the traits but for a comic theft, not loyal service.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli observes that everyone sees what a ruler appears to be, but few feel what he really is, and those few dare not contradict the many.
philosophy.explanation: Machiavelli stresses how far appearance can be separated from inner purpose in political life.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s spy depends on that gap: an unsuspected outward form hiding a fixed inner purpose.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares the appearance-versus-reality theme; Machiavelli applies it to princes, not spies.

kurals.tamil:
துறந்தார் படிவத்த ராகி இறந்தாராய்ந்து
என்செயினும் சோர்விலது ஒற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Thurandhaar padivaththa raagi irandhaaraaindhu
Enseyinum soarviladhu otru.
kurals.meaning: A spy takes on the guise of a renunciant, gets into places others cannot enter, investigates thoroughly, and never gives himself away, whatever is done to him.
kurals.elementary: In old stories, a clever messenger sometimes dresses as a humble traveller so he can pass through the gates. Even if guards question him roughly, he stays in character and keeps his secret. This kural describes that kind of brave, patient spy.
kurals.university: துறந்தார் படிவத்தர் ஆகி means ‘taking on the form (படிவம்) of those who have renounced’, that is, dressing as an ascetic or wandering monk. Such figures could travel freely in ancient India. இறந்து ஆராய்ந்து is read by Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘going beyond [ordinary limits], into places otherwise unreachable, and examining’. Pappaiah makes it explicit: places one cannot go. என்செயினும் சோர்வு இலது means ‘whatever [the suspicious] may do to him, he does not slip’. Here சோர்வு means a lapse that gives the secret away, not tiredness, and Pappaiah and Kalaignar both read it as holding out under torture. The disguise matches the Arthashastra’s tāpasa (ascetic) spy closely, which is often cited in comparative studies of the Kural. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give identical text; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi forms ராகி யிறந்தாராய்ந் / தென்செயினுஞ் சோர்வில தொற்று.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A man with shaved head (muṇḍa) or braided hair (jaṭila) and desirous to earn livelihood is a spy under the guise of an ascetic practising austerities. Such a spy surrounded by a host of disciples with shaved head or braided hair may take his abode in the suburbs of a city …”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya describes in detail the spy disguised as an ascetic, a figure respected enough to go anywhere and hear everything.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s துறந்தார் படிவம், the guise of a renunciant, almost exactly.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Direct match on the ascetic disguise; the Arthashastra does not stress endurance under torture here.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that a harmless religious appearance can hide a very different inner purpose.
christianity.tie_back: Seen from the other side, this is the Kural’s spy in a renunciant’s robe. Scripture condemns the deceit, while Valluvar approves of it for the service of a just state.
christianity._accuracy_note: Contrast parallel: same device of a religious disguise, opposite moral judgment.

islam.quote_or_event: On the freezing night of the Battle of the Trench, the Prophet sent Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman into the enemy camp for news, telling him to do nothing that would alarm them. Hudhayfah saw Abu Sufyan warming himself by a fire, held back from shooting him, and returned with his report.
islam.explanation: Hudhayfah went through cold and danger into the enemy’s midst, stayed undetected, and kept strictly to his mission.
islam.tie_back: He entered where others would not go, kept his cover, and did not break discipline, which is the Kural’s இறந்து ஆராய்ந்து … சோர்வு இலது.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong parallel on nerve and discipline; no ascetic disguise is involved.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And they went, and came unto the mountain, and abode there three days, until the pursuers were returned: and the pursuers sought them throughout all the way, but found them not.”
judaism.explanation: Joshua’s two spies, hunted after their mission in Jericho, hid patiently in the hills until it was safe to return with their report.
judaism.tie_back: Their patience and their refusal to be caught match the Kural’s spy who does not slip whatever happens.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good on endurance and evasion; there is no disguise as renunciants.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What is the use of your matted hair, O witless man? What of your garment of antelope’s hide? Within you is the tangle (of passion); only outwardly do you cleanse yourself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that ascetic dress, such as matted hair and hide garments, can be a mere outward costume over an unrenounced mind.
buddhism.tie_back: The verse shows how common it was for renunciant dress to be only a costume, the very disguise the Kural’s spy uses.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Contrast parallel on false ascetic appearance; the Buddha condemns it, while Valluvar uses it.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Helen recalls how Odysseus disfigured himself with blows, put on a beggar’s rags like a slave, and slipped into Troy. He went unrecognised by all but her, gathered much knowledge, and got back safely to the Greeks.
greek_mythology.explanation: The master spy of Greek legend takes on the humblest disguise, that of a beggar, to enter the enemy city.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A beggar’s disguise in Greece matches the renunciant’s disguise in the Kural: the lowest-status, least-suspected costume to get where others cannot.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close in method; a beggar replaces the ascetic.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus calls the true Cynic philosopher, who wears only a rough cloak and owns nothing, a ‘scout’ (kataskopos) sent ahead by God to spy out what is truly friendly or hostile to human beings and to report back fearlessly, as Diogenes did.
philosophy.explanation: Stoic teaching pictures the ascetic philosopher as a spy who goes into frightening territory and returns with a report that is not distorted by fear.
philosophy.tie_back: An ascetic who is really a scout and cannot be shaken is the Kural’s spy, turned into a moral image.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Remarkable image-level match; the ‘spying’ is metaphorical and spiritual.

kurals.tamil:
மறைந்தவை கேட்கவற் றாகி அறிந்தவை
ஐயப்பாடு இல்லதே ஒற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Maraindhavai kaetkavat raagi arindhavai
Aiyappaadu illadhae otru.
kurals.meaning: A spy is one who can draw out what is hidden and who is left with no doubt about what he has found.
kurals.elementary: A good detective in a mystery story does two things: she finds the hidden clues, and she checks them until she is sure before she tells anyone. Guessing isn’t enough. This kural says a real investigator uncovers secrets and makes sure they are true.
kurals.university: மறைந்தவை கேட்க வற்று ஆகி means ‘being able (வற்று, ‘capable’) to hear what is concealed’. அறிந்தவை ஐயப்பாடு இல்லது means ‘having no doubt about what has been learned’. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the second half as being able to decide firmly without wavering. Pappaiah adds that the spy draws secrets ‘from the very mouth of those who did the deed’, and Kalaignar that he learns through those who are present at secret meetings. So the couplet sets two standards, access to secrets and certainty about them, and the next two couplets (588-589) add a check on that certainty from the king’s side. The text is identical across the three sources, apart from the sandhi யறிந்தவை / யையப்பா டில்லதே in thirukkural-thamizh.org.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A skilful person capable of guessing the mind of others is a fraudulent disciple. Having encouraged such a spy with honour and money rewards, the minister shall tell him, ‘Sworn to the king and myself, thou shalt inform us of whatever wickedness thou findest in others.’”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya’s first class of spy is chosen for his skill at reading hidden intentions and is bound by oath to report them.
hinduism.tie_back: Reading what others hide is the Kural’s மறைந்தவை கேட்க வற்று.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on uncovering the hidden; the certainty requirement is handled elsewhere in Kautilya (1.12).

christianity.quote_or_event: “For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known. Therefore whatsoever ye have spoken in darkness shall be heard in the light; and that which ye have spoken in the ear in closets shall be proclaimed upon the housetops.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that whispered secrets will eventually be heard and brought into the open.
christianity.tie_back: Secrets told ‘in the ear in closets’ are exactly the மறைந்தவை the Kural’s spy is able to hear.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the idea that hidden speech comes out; it is a moral warning, not spycraft.

islam.quote_or_event: “And a man came from the farthest end of the city, running. He said, ‘O Moses, indeed the eminent ones are conferring over you [intending] to kill you, so leave [the city]; indeed, I am to you of the sincere advisors.’”
islam.explanation: A well-wisher learns of the chiefs’ secret plot and rushes to warn Moses with a clear, certain report.
islam.tie_back: He learns a closed council’s hidden plan and delivers it without hesitation, as the Kural’s ideal informant would.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on uncovering and reporting a secret plot; the man is a volunteer, not a commissioned spy.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And one of his servants said, None, my lord, O king: but Elisha, the prophet that is in Israel, telleth the king of Israel the words that thou speakest in thy bedchamber.”
judaism.explanation: The king of Aram suspects a traitor because Israel always knows his plans, and learns that the prophet Elisha reveals even words spoken in his bedchamber.
judaism.tie_back: Knowing ‘the words spoken in the bedchamber’ is the furthest reach of the Kural’s hearing of hidden things.
judaism._accuracy_note: Vivid match on penetrating secrets; the source is prophetic insight, not human espionage.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Mahā-Ummagga Jātaka, the sage Mahosadha’s trained parrot, sent to the court of King Cūḷani-Brahmadatta, overhears the king and his chaplain Kevaṭṭa secretly plotting to conquer all of India and brings the plan back to his master.
buddhism.explanation: The Jātaka shows a hidden plot being discovered and reported with certainty in time for the wise minister to act.
buddhism.tie_back: The parrot overhears what was meant to stay hidden, which is the Kural’s ideal of hearing the concealed.
buddhism.source: Mahā-Ummagga Jātaka (Jātaka 546), as summarised in the Dictionary of Pali Proper Names (paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: A close narrative parallel told as a fable; checked against a reference summary.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Demeter searches everywhere for her stolen daughter, it is Helios, the Sun who watches over gods and men, who tells her the hidden truth: Zeus had given Persephone to Hades, who carried her off to the underworld.
greek_mythology.explanation: Only the all-seeing Sun knows the concealed deed, and he reports it plainly and with certainty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Helios has what the Kural requires: access to what is hidden and an account free of doubt.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good on hidden-truth-revealed; Helios is a witness-god, not an agent sent on a mission.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Descartes’ first rule of method is never to accept anything as true that he does not clearly know to be so, and to include nothing in his judgments beyond what is presented to his mind so clearly and distinctly that he has no occasion to doubt it.
philosophy.explanation: Descartes makes freedom from doubt the test for accepting any proposition.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ஐயப்பாடு இல்லது (‘free of doubt’) applies the same standard to a spy’s findings.
philosophy.source: René Descartes, Discourse on Method, Part 2 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the certainty half only; Descartes is concerned with philosophical knowledge, not intelligence.

kurals.tamil:
ஒற்றொற்றித் தந்த பொருளையும் மற்றுமோர்
ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றிக் கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Otrotrith thandha porulaiyum matrumoar
Otrinaal otrik kolal.
kurals.meaning: Even information a spy has gathered and brought in should be accepted only after it has been checked by another spy.
kurals.elementary: If one friend tells you there is no school tomorrow, you would probably check with another friend or the school website before staying home. This kural says a wise leader always double-checks a report with a second source.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on the root ஒற்று, which appears four times (ஒற்று ஒற்றித் தந்த … ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றி): ‘what a spy has spied out and delivered, have it spied out again by another spy, and then accept it’. The உம் in பொருளையும் (‘even the information’) means that even a reliable spy’s report is not exempt. Mu. Varadarasanar says it should be taken as true only after the two accounts are found to agree (ஒப்புமை கண்டபின்). Kalaignar stresses comparing the two reports before deciding. கொளல் is an infinitive-style imperative (‘one should accept’), the same form Valluvar uses for maxims elsewhere. This couplet and 589 together set out a clear doctrine of corroborating intelligence. The text agrees across all three sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The immediate officers of the institutes of espionage (saṃsthānāmantevāsina) shall, by making use of signs or writing (saṃjñā lipibhi), set their own spies in motion (to ascertain the validity of the information).”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya builds a second layer of spies whose job is to check the reports of the first.
hinduism.tie_back: Spies sent to test other spies’ information are the Kural’s மற்றுமோர் ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றிக் கொளல் put into practice.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-identical rule; the parenthetical gloss is the translator’s.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the church to test every claim before holding on to it.
christianity.tie_back: Test first, then accept: the Kural’s rule for spy reports in its most general form.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good general principle; it concerns spiritual claims and does not specify a second witness.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, if there comes to you a disobedient one with information, investigate, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and become, over what you have done, regretful.”
islam.explanation: The Quran orders that a report from an unreliable source be investigated before anyone acts on it, to avoid harming innocent people.
islam.tie_back: Verify before acting, especially where lives are at stake: the heart of this Kural.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close; the Quran specifies an unreliable informant, while the Kural checks even trusted spies.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then shalt thou enquire, and make search, and ask diligently; and, behold, if it be truth, and the thing certain …”
judaism.explanation: Deuteronomy says that a rumour of grave wrongdoing in a town must be investigated thoroughly and found true and certain before anything is done.
judaism.tie_back: Enquire, search and ask diligently until it is certain: the Kural’s demand for a second check.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on verification before action; it does not specify a second independent informant.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Come, Kalamas. Do not go upon what has been acquired by repeated hearing; nor upon tradition; nor upon rumor; nor upon what is in a scripture; nor upon surmise …”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the Kalamas not to accept a claim just because it was reported to them, but to test it until they know for themselves.
buddhism.tie_back: Refusing to act on a report alone is the Kural’s refusal to accept even one spy’s word unchecked.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 3.65, Kalama Sutta (trans. Soma Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the principle of not trusting unverified report; it is about doctrines, not intelligence.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Trojans capture the Greek Sinon, who tells a moving story that the wooden horse is a sacred offering. Without checking his story against any other source, and ignoring Laocoön’s warning, they drag the horse into the city, and Troy falls.
greek_mythology.explanation: The most famous intelligence failure in myth comes from trusting one planted informant.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the disaster the Kural guards against by never accepting a single source unchecked.
greek_mythology.source: Virgil, Aeneid 2 (paraphrase; the story belongs to the Greek Trojan cycle)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clear negative example; the fullest surviving telling is Roman, not Greek.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Without subtle ingenuity of mind, one cannot make certain of the truth of their reports.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu warns that spy reports cannot simply be taken at face value; the ruler must use his judgment to test them.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts insist that a spy’s report must be tested before it is trusted.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 13.17 (trans. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Same concern; Sun Tzu relies on the ruler’s insight rather than a second spy.

kurals.tamil:
ஒற்றெற் றுணராமை ஆள்க உடன்மூவர்
சொற்றொக்க தேறப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Otret runaraamai aalga udanmoovar
Sotrokka thaerap padum.
kurals.meaning: Employ spies so that none of them knows about the others; when the reports of three such spies agree, the matter can be trusted.
kurals.elementary: If three students are each asked separately what happened at recess, and they can’t talk to each other first, but all three tell the same story, the teacher can be pretty sure it is true. This kural says a wise leader checks the truth the same way.
kurals.university: The first line says to employ (ஆள்க) spies in a way that one does not become aware (உணராமை) of another. The second says that when the words of three (மூவர் சொல்) agree together (தொக்க), the thing may be trusted (தேறப்படும்). There is a real textual variant in the first word. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print ஒற்றெற் றுணராமை, while thirukkural-thamizh.org prints ஒற்றொற் றுணராமை, i.e. ஒற்று ஒற்று உணராமை, ‘one spy not knowing another spy’. That is the sense every commentator, including Parimelazhagar, gives, and the -எற்று form is best explained as a sandhi or scribal variant. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the second line as ‘if the three agree, take it as true’. Pappaiah is more cautious: even when three agree, examine it before accepting. The rule is strikingly close to Arthashastra 1.12, which requires agreement from three independent sources and says the spy-units must not know one another.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Neither the institutes of espionage nor they (the wandering spies) shall know each other … When the information thus received from these three different sources is exactly of the same version, it shall be held reliable. If they (the three sources) frequently differ, the spies concerned shall either be punished in secret or dismissed.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya requires spy networks that do not know one another and accepts a report only when three independent sources agree.
hinduism.tie_back: Spies unaware of one another and three agreeing sources: both halves of the Kural, point for point.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Essentially the same rule; one of the closest Kural–Arthashastra correspondences.

christianity.quote_or_event: In the story of Susanna, the young Daniel separates the two elders who have falsely accused her and questions each alone about which tree the alleged act happened under. One says a mastic tree and the other a holm oak, their lie is exposed, and Susanna is saved.
christianity.explanation: By keeping the witnesses apart, Daniel makes sure their stories are truly independent, so their disagreement shows the truth.
christianity.tie_back: Keeping informants from knowing one another and then comparing their words is the Kural’s method exactly.
christianity.source: Susanna (Daniel 13 in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles; KJV Apocrypha), vv. 51-59 (paraphrase)
christianity._accuracy_note: Excellent procedural match; it is canonical for Catholic and Orthodox Christians and deuterocanonical for Protestants.

islam.quote_or_event: “And bring to witness two witnesses from among your men … That is more just in the sight of Allāh and stronger as evidence and more likely to prevent doubt between you.”
islam.explanation: The Quran requires more than one witness for important transactions, because corroboration strengthens evidence and removes doubt.
islam.tie_back: Several witnesses to remove doubt reflects the Kural’s agreement of three.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the corroboration principle; the context is recording debts, not intelligence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And afterward they bring in the second witness and examine him in the same manner. If their statements are found to be congruent the judges then discuss the matter.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah requires witnesses to be questioned one at a time with the others sent out of the room, and their testimony counts only if their separate accounts agree.
judaism.tie_back: Separate examination so that no witness knows another’s answer, followed by a check for agreement, is the Kural’s procedure in a courtroom.
judaism.source: Mishnah Sanhedrin 3:6 (William Davidson / Koren-Steinsaltz translation, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Near-identical method; it applies to legal witnesses and not spies, and requires two rather than three.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Without approval and without scorn, but carefully studying the sentences word by word, one should trace them in the Discourses and verify them by the Discipline.”
buddhism.explanation: In the ‘four great references’, the Buddha says that any claim to be his teaching must be checked against two independent standards, the Suttas and the Vinaya, before it is accepted.
buddhism.tie_back: Accepting a report only when independent sources agree is the principle behind the Kural’s three agreeing spies.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahāparinibbāna Sutta 4.8-11 (trans. Sister Vajira & Francis Story)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the cross-verification logic; it concerns the authenticity of doctrine.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: To test the oracles, King Croesus sent separate messengers to several shrines at once, each to ask on the hundredth day what the king was doing at that moment. Only Delphi (and, by some accounts, Amphiaraus) answered correctly, that he was boiling a tortoise and lamb in a bronze pot.
greek_mythology.explanation: Croesus set up independent, simultaneous inquiries so that the sources could not coordinate, then trusted only those that proved accurate.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Independent informants who cannot confer, judged by whether their answers match reality, is the Kural’s method in legendary form.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clever procedural parallel; Croesus tests the sources rather than the agreement among them.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Thucydides says he did not rely on the first account he heard or on his own impressions, but tested every report as rigorously as he could, which was hard because different eyewitnesses gave differing accounts of the same events.
philosophy.explanation: The founder of critical history describes his method as cross-examining several independent witnesses.
philosophy.tie_back: Comparing independent reports and accepting only what holds up is what the Kural asks of a king.
philosophy.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 1.22 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong methodological parallel; Thucydides sets no fixed number such as three.

kurals.tamil:
சிறப்பறிய ஒற்றின்கண் செய்யற்க செய்யின்
புறப்படுத்தான் ஆகும் மறை.
kurals.transliteration:
Sirapariya otrinkan seyyarka seyyin
Purappaduththaan aagum marai.
kurals.meaning: A king should not honour a spy where others can see; if he does, he himself will have given away the secret.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a secret helper who quietly tells the teacher when someone is being picked on. If the teacher gave that helper a big prize in front of the whole class, everyone would know who the helper was, and the secret would be ruined. This kural says to thank secret helpers quietly.
kurals.university: சிறப்பு அறிய means ‘so that the honour is known [to others]’; ஒற்றின்கண் செய்யற்க, ‘do not do it to the spy’; செய்யின் புறப்படுத்தான் ஆகும் மறை, ‘if you do, you become the one who brought the secret out into the open (புறப்படுத்தல்)’. The irony is that after all the care in 585-589 to keep spies hidden, the king himself becomes the leak by rewarding them publicly. Pappaiah reads the couplet as ‘reward the spy, but reward him secretly’, which fits Sun Tzu’s and Kautilya’s view that spies must be generously paid. Mu. Varadarasanar reads மறை as both the secret information and the spy’s identity. The text agrees across sources; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi form வொற்றின்கட் செய்யற்க செய்யிற் / புறப்படுத்தா னாகு மறை.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That king whose secret plans other people, (though) assembled (for the purpose), do not discover, (will) enjoy the whole earth, though he be poor in treasure.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu puts keeping counsel secret above wealth as a source of royal power.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s warning about leaking the secret through public honours protects exactly this kind of secrecy.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on the value of secrecy; it does not mention rewarding spies.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that good deeds and gifts should be given quietly, without public display.
christianity.tie_back: Giving in secret instead of in public view is the Kural’s advice on how to reward a spy.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on hidden giving; the motive is humility, not operational security.

islam.quote_or_event: “If you disclose your charitable expenditures, they are good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you, and He will remove from you some of your misdeeds [thereby].”
islam.explanation: The Quran allows open giving but calls concealed giving better.
islam.tie_back: Its preference for concealed giving matches the Kural’s preference for a spy’s reward given out of sight.
islam._accuracy_note: Parallel on concealed giving; the reason is spiritual sincerity, not secrecy.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the gossip who exposes secrets with the trustworthy person who keeps them.
judaism.tie_back: A king who honours his spy publicly acts like the ‘talebearer’ who reveals secrets, and the Kural wants him to be the faithful one who keeps them.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good on guarding secrets; not about rewards or spies specifically.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the standard description of right speech, the disciple does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard in one place in order to divide people, nor repeat here what he has heard there.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist ethics teaches restraint in passing on what one has heard, to avoid causing harm and division.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural also asks the king not to let slip, through a public gesture, what should stay unspoken.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 41, Sāleyyaka Sutta, on right speech (paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Only a loose parallel on discretion; the Buddhist rule targets divisive speech.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas’s barber, the only one who knew his master had donkey’s ears, could not bear to keep the secret. He whispered it into a hole in the ground and covered it, but reeds grew there and whispered the secret to the wind for everyone to hear.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows that a secret, once let out in any form, finds its way to everyone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural warns the king not to be the one who lets it out, by a gesture as small as a public reward.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Shares the leaked-secret theme; the leak is by a servant, not by honouring an agent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Hence it is that which none in the whole army are more intimate relations to be maintained than with spies. None should be more liberally rewarded. In no other business should greater secrecy be preserved.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu joins generous rewards for spies with the strictest secrecy in handling them.
philosophy.tie_back: Reward richly but in secret is exactly the balance this Kural asks for.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 13.14 (trans. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one pairing of reward and secrecy; the grammatical slip is in Giles’s original.
